vignette:
Mohan's hands, gnarled by seventy years of work, move with a muscle memory that predates his own conscious thought. At the wheel, he is a creator, a master of earth and water. But lately, the clay feels foreign, slick and cold under his touch. He says the memories began to surface with the rains this year, but in our sessions, it becomes clear they have always been there, just beneath the surface, like stones in a riverbed.

He was four years old, perhaps five-no one is certain-when his world was cleaved in two. He doesn't remember the politics, only the heat and the smoke. His narrative of 1947 is not a story but a collage of sensory fragments. The suffocating crush of bodies at the Lahore train station. The metallic taste of fear in his mouth. The high-pitched wail of a woman who had lost her child in the crowd. He remembers his mother's hand, a vise on his small wrist, and the constant, urgent whisper of his father: "Stay close. Do not let go."

His most vivid memory, the one that jolts him from sleep, is of his older brother, Sameer, who was seven. Sameer, with his mischievous grin, had a small wooden toy train. In the chaos of boarding the real train, the toy slipped from Sameer's grasp and fell between the platform and the carriage. Sameer instinctively reached for it. Mohan remembers the lurch of the train, his father's desperate shout, and then... nothing. His mind has sealed off the image, but not the feeling-a hollow emptiness that settled in his chest and has never quite left.

They arrived in Delhi with nothing but the clothes on their backs and a silence that consumed his parents. His father, also a potter, set up a makeshift wheel in the refugee camp. He never spoke of Sameer, but his grief was fired into every pot he threw. Mohan learned the craft from him, not through words, but through watching and imitating. The spinning clay became his language, a way to shape the formless sorrow into something solid, something useful. For decades, it worked. He built a life, married his wife, Anjali, and raised two children. The studio was his sanctuary, a place where the ghosts of the past were kept at bay by the rhythmic hum of the wheel.

The cracks began to show subtly. He stopped watching the evening news; the images of refugees fleeing conflict in other parts of the world were too much to bear. He'd flinch violently at the sound of a car backfiring, his hand flying to his chest. Anjali mentions his nightmares have grown more frequent, filled with the grinding sound of train wheels and muffled shouting. He has become withdrawn, spending more and more time in his studio, yet producing less. He will sit before a lump of clay for hours, his hands resting on the still wheel, his gaze fixed on a past he cannot escape.

Last month, his grandson, a joyful, boisterous boy of seven, ran into the studio and tripped, sending a row of freshly thrown pots crashing to the floor. The sharp, shattering sound sent Mohan stumbling backward, his face ashen. He didn't see his grandson or the broken pottery. He saw a small wooden toy splintering on the tracks. He yelled, a raw, guttural sound that terrified the boy and brought Anjali running. He couldn't explain it to her then, couldn't give voice to the terror that had seized him. He just stood there, a 75-year-old man, trembling in the wreckage of the present, trapped in the ruins of a memory from a lifetime ago.
